positions/design-argument-paley/oneLine: The intricate adaptation of means to ends in nature — like a watch found on a heath — points to an intelligent and benevolent Designer.
positions/design-argument-paley/coreClai: Complex, functional order demands an intelligent cause.
Living organisms display contrivance far exceeding human artefacts.
The argument is empirical, cumulative and accessible to ordinary people.
Design reveals God’s wisdom and goodness.
positions/design-argument-paley/origin: Ancient roots (Cicero, Aquinas’ fifth way); flourished in English “physico-theology” (John Ray, 1691; Robert Boyle) and culminated in William Paley’s Natural Theology (1802) and the Bridgewater Treatises (1833-36).
positions/design-argument-paley/stronges: It argues from publicly observable features of nature.
It harmonised Christianity with the scientific revolution.
Fine-tuning versions remain influential in cosmology.
Hume objected that the analogy is weak and the conclusion falls short of the God of theism.
Darwin’s natural selection explained adaptation without foresight, undercutting biological design arguments.
Barthians and Kierkegaardians argue that a designer-God is not the God revealed in Christ.
positions/design-argument-paley/response: Defenders reply that cosmic fine-tuning and the lawfulness that natural selection itself presupposes still point to design.
Intelligent-design advocates revived biological design at the molecular level.
positions/design-argument-paley/conseque: Its eclipse shaped later suspicion of natural theology and the rise of intelligent design.
positions/barthian-rejection-natural-the: Barth’s “No!”: revelation only in Christ
rejection of natural theology
Christocentric revelation
Nein!
There is no knowledge of God apart from God’s self-revelation in Jesus Christ, attested in Scripture; natural theology is not a preparation for faith but a human attempt to master God.
God is known only through God: revelation is God’s free act, not a human capacity.
Jesus Christ is the one Word of God (Barmen thesis 1).
There is no “point of contact” in fallen humanity that grace can build on.
Natural theology leads to idolatries such as the German Christians’ “God of blood and soil”.
John 1:18
John 14:6
Matthew 11:27
1 Corinthians 1:18-25
Colossians 2:3

Developed by Karl Barth from Romans (1919/1922) onward and crystallised in the Barmen Declaration and Nein! (1934); continued in Church Dogmatics I/1-2 (1932-38), though later Barth spoke of “little lights” in creation (CD IV/3, 1959).
Eduard Thurneysen
Barmen Declaration
Many post-war European Reformed theologians
It keeps theology accountable to the concrete revelation in Christ rather than to culture or ideology.
It was vindicated historically by the church struggle against Nazism.
It takes seriously the noetic effects of sin.
Brunner, Catholics and many evangelicals argue it cannot do justice to Psalm 19, Acts 17 and Romans 1-2.
Critics say it isolates faith from public reason and science (“fideism”).
Some argue Barth later softened his view, making the 1934 polemic overstated.
Barthians answer that Romans 1 speaks of knowledge that condemns because it is suppressed, not a usable foundation.
T. F. Torrance reformulated natural theology within revealed theology rather than as its foundation.
Defined neo-orthodox theology.
Influenced Protestant suspicion of apologetics and of civil religion.
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/name: Brunner’s “point of contact” and limited natural revelation
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/oneLi: Although sinners cannot know God savingly apart from Christ, God’s revelation in creation is real, and humanity retains a formal image — its responsibility and capacity to be addressed — that serves as a point of contact for the gospel.
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/coreC: Creation is a genuine revelation of God, though fallen humans distort it.
The material image (righteousness) was lost; the formal image (personhood, addressability) remains.
Grace does not destroy but restores nature.
Calvin himself taught a revelation in creation and a sense of deity.
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/origi: Set out in Emil Brunner’s Nature and Grace (1934), appealing to Calvin; developed in his Revelation and Reason (1941).
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/propo: Many later evangelical theologians of general revelation
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/stron: It fits the biblical texts on revelation in creation and conscience.
It stands in continuity with Calvin.
It makes missionary communication intelligible: there is something in the hearer to address.
Barth argued that any point of contact becomes a human possession that relativises grace and invites ideological natural theologies.
Catholic critics found Brunner too negative about natural reason.
Some argue “formal image” is too thin to do the work Brunner wants.
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/respo: Brunner replied that the point of contact is created by God and is no merit, and that denying it makes human responsibility unintelligible.
He noted that Barth’s own practice presupposes hearers capable of understanding language.
positions/brunner-point-of-contact/conse: Shaped mediating Protestant and evangelical theologies of general revelation.
Remains a reference point in missiology.
positions/reformed-epistemology/oneLine: Belief in God can be rational and warranted without being based on arguments, just as belief in other minds or the past is; it can be “properly basic”, produced by a God-given faculty (the sensus divinitatis) and the witness of the Spirit.
positions/reformed-epistemology/coreClai: Classical foundationalism (only self-evident or evident-to-the-senses beliefs are basic) is self-refuting.
Belief in God may be basic, formed in appropriate circumstances such as wonder, guilt or gratitude.
If Christianity is true, Christian belief is probably warranted.
Arguments are helpful but not necessary for rational faith.
positions/reformed-epistemology/origin: Developed by Alvin Plantinga and Nicholas Wolterstorff (Faith and Rationality, 1983), drawing on Calvin’s sensus divinitatis and Thomas Reid; culminating in Plantinga’s Warranted Christian Belief (2000).
positions/reformed-epistemology/stronges: It explains how ordinary believers without philosophical training can be rational.
It exposes the double standard of evidentialist objections.
It recovers Calvin’s teaching on the sense of the divine and the Spirit’s testimony.
Critics raise the “Great Pumpkin” objection: could any belief be called properly basic?
Evidentialists argue it shields belief from rational scrutiny and is close to fideism.
Religious diversity seems to give defeaters for basic belief.
positions/reformed-epistemology/response: Plantinga answers that proper basicality depends on properly functioning faculties in appropriate circumstances, not arbitrary choice.
Reformed epistemologists acknowledge defeaters and engage in “negative apologetics” to rebut them.
positions/reformed-epistemology/conseque: Transformed philosophy of religion from the 1980s.
Influenced evangelical, Catholic and Jewish epistemology.
positions/classical-apologetics/oneLine: Apologetics proceeds in two steps: first, natural theology establishes that God exists; then historical evidences (fulfilled prophecy, miracles, the resurrection) show that this God has revealed himself in Christ.
positions/classical-apologetics/coreClai: Theism must be established before miracles can be recognised as divine acts.
Cosmological, teleological, moral and ontological arguments provide that foundation.
Historical evidence then confirms Christianity specifically.
Reason is common ground with unbelievers.
positions/classical-apologetics/origin: Pattern of Aquinas’ Summa contra Gentiles (c.1260) and post-Reformation apologists; revived by R. C. Sproul, John Gerstner and Arthur Lindsley (Classical Apologetics, 1984), Norman Geisler and William Lane Craig; the kalām argument draws on medieval Islamic theology.
positions/classical-apologetics/stronges: It follows the natural order of argument: who God is before what God has done.
It stands in the long tradition of Aquinas and Anselm.
It is effective in public debate.
Presuppositionalists argue it grants the unbeliever’s autonomous reason as neutral judge.
Evidentialists argue the two steps are unnecessary: the resurrection evidence can establish both at once.
Kierkegaardians argue that proven probability cannot ground passionate faith.
positions/classical-apologetics/response: Classical apologists reply that reason is God-given and shared, not autonomous, and that their arguments appeal to what unbelievers already know.
They argue that without theism, miracles can always be reinterpreted naturalistically.
positions/classical-apologetics/conseque: Shapes much evangelical apologetics ministry and campus debate.
Revived interest in medieval and Islamic philosophy (kalām).
positions/evidential-apologetics/oneLine: Christianity can be defended directly from historical and empirical evidence — especially the resurrection of Jesus, fulfilled prophecy and miracles — which shows both that God exists and that he has acted in Christ.
positions/evidential-apologetics/coreCla: The resurrection is a historical event that can be investigated.
Miracles function as evidence for God and for Christ’s claims.
Probability is the guide of life; certainty is not required.
The method is open-ended and empirical.
positions/evidential-apologetics/origin: Prepared by Grotius (1627) and Butler’s Analogy (1736), Paley’s Evidences (1794) and Simon Greenleaf (1846); revived by John Warwick Montgomery, Gary Habermas and the “minimal facts” approach.
positions/evidential-apologetics/stronge: The New Testament itself appeals to eyewitness evidence (1 Corinthians 15).
It engages modern people on their own empirical terms.
It does not require prior acceptance of philosophical arguments.
Presuppositionalists argue that facts are interpreted by worldviews, so evidence alone cannot persuade a committed naturalist.
Hume and later sceptics argue miracles are always the least probable explanation.
Kierkegaard argued that historical probability cannot ground eternal commitment.
positions/evidential-apologetics/respons: Evidentialists answer that worldview-dependence is not total and evidence can force revision of worldviews.
They argue Hume’s objection assumes naturalism and that the resurrection hypothesis best explains the minimal facts.
positions/evidential-apologetics/consequ: Dominant in popular evangelical apologetics (Evidence That Demands a Verdict, 1972; The Case for Christ, 1998).
positions/presuppositional-apologetics/o: There is no neutral ground between belief and unbelief; the apologist should presuppose the truth of Scripture and show that only the Christian worldview provides the preconditions for logic, science and morality, which unbelievers borrow.
positions/presuppositional-apologetics/c: All reasoning rests on ultimate presuppositions.
Unbelievers know God but suppress the truth (Romans 1:18).
The transcendental argument: without the triune God, nothing is intelligible.
Apologetics must not grant human reason autonomy over God’s Word.
positions/presuppositional-apologetics/o: Developed by Cornelius Van Til at Westminster Theological Seminary (The Defense of the Faith, 1955), building on Abraham Kuyper’s antithesis; popularised by Greg Bahnsen (debate with Gordon Stein, 1985), John Frame and Gordon Clark (rationalist variant).
positions/presuppositional-apologetics/s: It takes the noetic effects of sin and the authority of Scripture seriously.
It exposes hidden assumptions in secular reasoning.
It is internally consistent with Reformed theology.
Classical and evidential apologists argue it is circular and can only preach to the converted.
Critics say the transcendental argument has never been rigorously formulated.
Some argue Van Til misread Aquinas and Butler.
positions/presuppositional-apologetics/r: Presuppositionalists answer that every ultimate standard is circular in a broad sense; the question is which circle is coherent.
Frame has modified the approach to include evidence within a presuppositional framework.
positions/presuppositional-apologetics/c: Influential in conservative Reformed and some Baptist circles.
Shaped Christian Reconstructionist thought through Rushdoony and Bahnsen.
